title: De lineis curvis non in eodem plano sitis, quae maximi minimive proprietate sunt praeditae

deep.reconstruction:
Problem II of E740 asks for a space curve (x, y(x), z(x)) that makes the functional ∫(y+z) dy dz/dx = ∫(y+z) y' z' dx stationary. Write p = y' and q = z'. The integrand is V = pq(y+z). Its partial derivatives are M = V_x = 0, N = V_y = pq, N' = V_z = pq, P = V_p = (y+z)q and P' = V_q = (y+z)p. Euler's general scheme for two dependent variables gives three equations:
(1) M dx = dS, with S = V − pP − qP' = −pq(y+z). This is the Beltrami/energy first integral, valid because the integrand does not depend on x.
(2) N dx = dP and (3) N' dx = dP'. These are the two Euler–Lagrange equations.
Step 1. Equation (1) gives pq(y+z) = a, so y+z = a/(pq). Then (y+z)q = a/p and (y+z)p = a/q.
Step 2. The Euler–Lagrange equations become pq dx = −a dp/p² = −a dq/q². Hence dp/p² = dq/q², so 1/q = 1/p + 1/c (Euler writes b and absorbs the sign), i.e. q = cp/(c+p).
Step 3. Then y+z = a(c+p)/(cp²) and dx = −a(c+p)dp/(cp⁴), which integrates to x = a/(3p³) + a/(2cp²) + f.
Step 4 (next page). y = a/(2p²) + a/(cp) + g and z = a/(2p²) − g. There are four constants a, c, f, g, matching two second-order Euler–Lagrange equations. Euler argues the curve is non-planar and algebraic, and gives its projection on the y–z plane as the parabola 2a(z+g) = c²(y−z−2g)².
In the parameter u = 1/p the extremal is a polynomial curve of degrees (3, 2, 2): an affine twisted cubic. The page belongs to Euler's late programme of extending the Methodus inveniendi (1744) to curves of double curvature, i.e. problems with two unknown functions.
errors: No computational errors. Every step checks: x' = −a(c+p)/(cp⁴) integrates to a/(3p³) + a/(2cp²); also dz = q dx = −a dp/p³, consistent with z = a/(2p²) − g on the next page.
Sign of the constant: −1/p = −1/q + b gives 1/p = 1/q − b, not 1/p = 1/q + b. This is harmless because b is arbitrary, and q = cp/(c+p) is consistent with 1/q = 1/p + 1/c.

Conceptual gap: Euler calls the curve one where the integral attains a 'maximum minimumve'. The Hessian of V in (p, q) is (y+z)·[[0,1],[1,0]], which is indefinite everywhere. So the Legendre condition fails and the extremal can be neither a maximum nor a minimum (a saddle). Euler only finds stationary curves.

Euler uses the first integral (1) together with both Euler–Lagrange equations. These are not independent, since (1) follows from (2) and (3). He does not remark on this, though his constant count of four is nonetheless correct.

ideas.what: Euler–Lagrange equations for a functional of two unknown functions y(x), z(x) (space curves)
ideas.modern_name: Euler–Lagrange system for several dependent variables
ideas.where_published: E740 itself; the related general principle is in Lagrange's 1760s δ-method papers; unsure about Euler's earlier explicit treatments

ideas.what: First integral S = V − pV_p − qV_q = const when V does not depend on x
Extremal of ∫(y+z)y'z'dx is the rational polynomial space curve x = a/3·u³ + a/(2c)·u² + f, y = a/2·u² + a/c·u + g, z = a/2·u² − g
ideas.usually_credited_to: twisted cubics studied systematically by Möbius (1827), Chasles (1837)
ideas.where_published: E740 (published 1813), next page, where it is called algebraic and non-planar but not identified as a cubic

missed.claim: Euler's solution curve is a twisted cubic (polynomial of degree 3 in u = 1/p), an early explicit appearance of a non-planar algebraic space curve of degree 3 arising from a variational problem. Euler only remarks that it is algebraic and non-planar.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Only a historical footnote to the prehistory of the twisted cubic, before Möbius and Chasles; of minor interest.

missed.claim: The integrand pq(y+z) has an indefinite (p, q)-Hessian, so no genuine maximum or minimum exists. Euler's 'maximum minimumve' is really a saddle-type stationary curve.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This illustrates that second-variation (Legendre) considerations were absent in Euler's multi-variable work. It is well known in general, so it is not a discovery.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine worked example of the Euler–Lagrange system for space curves, and it is correct. The only mildly notable feature is that the extremal is an explicit twisted cubic, which Euler does not identify as such. This is minor and already published in 1813.
transcription_corrections: The transcription matches the image well. 'consequenter −1/p = −1/q + b, sive 1/p = 1/q + b' is as printed; the second form contains a sign slip in the original, which is harmless since b is arbitrary.
